understand how human activities contribute to greenhouse gases

primer.text: Five gases do the trapping: water vapour, carbon dioxide, methane, CFCs and nitrous oxides. This note defines what makes a greenhouse gas, lists the main gases, and shows which human activities, from fossil fuel burning to cattle and rice paddies, release them.

lessons.title: The Gases That Trap Heat
lessons.opening: A greenhouse gas absorbs infrared radiation and keeps it in the atmosphere, and five gases matter most: water vapour, carbon dioxide, methane, CFCs and nitrous oxides, with fossil fuel burning and cattle farming driving the two most famous up.
keyPoints: A greenhouse gas absorbs infrared radiation so heat stays trapped in the atmosphere.
Water vapour, carbon dioxide, methane, CFCs and nitrous oxides are the main greenhouse gases.
Rising levels of these gases raise the average temperature of the Earth.
Burning fossil fuels produces carbon dioxide, while cattle digestion and rice paddy fields release methane.

low.restatement: Heat leaves as infrared, the special five gases soak it up, and our farms and factories release two of them fastest.
low.analogy: A roof that lets light in but holds warmth in — and the five shingles that do the holding.
low.examPointer: Learn the five-gas list, then pair carbon dioxide with fossil fuels and methane with cattle and paddies.

medium.restatement: The defining action is infrared absorption: these gases let sunlight land but intercept the outgoing heat, so rising levels warm the planet; the human fingerprint is specific, with combustion of fossil fuels emitting carbon dioxide and both cattle digestion and rice paddy fields emitting methane.
medium.analogy: Five sponges in the ceiling of a bathroom — sunlight drips through fine, but the steam never escapes.
medium.examPointer: Attribute each gas to its source; mixing up methane sources with carbon dioxide sources loses marks.

options.text: It absorbs infrared radiation, keeping heat trapped in the atmosphere
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: It reflects all sunlight back instantly
options.explanation: Absorption of infrared, not reflection of sunlight, defines it.
Rainfall is unrelated to the definition.
The defining action is trapping heat, not cooling.

options.text: Water vapour, carbon dioxide, methane, CFCs and nitrous oxides
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
The bulk atmosphere does not absorb infrared this way.
Noble gases are not greenhouse gases.
Neither belongs to the greenhouse list.

check.stem: Which human activity raises carbon dioxide levels?

options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Paddy fields release methane, not carbon dioxide.
Cattle release methane during digestion.
Salt mining is not the named source.

check.stem: Methane reaches the atmosphere from which two named sources?

options.text: Cattle digesting grass and rice paddy fields
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Those emit carbon dioxide and other pollutants, not the named methane sources.
Neither is the named human-linked source here.
CFCs, not methane, come from such uses.

check.stem: Why do rising greenhouse gas levels worry biologists?

options.text: Because more trapped heat raises the average temperature of the Earth
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: Because the gases poison plants directly
options.explanation: The concern is heat trapping, not direct poisoning.

options.text: Because they dissolve the ozone layer
options.explanation: Ozone depletion is a separate problem.
Acid rain comes from sulfur dioxide, a different issue.

check.stem: State what a greenhouse gas does.
check.modelAnswer: A greenhouse gas absorbs infrared radiation so heat remains trapped in the atmosphere of the Earth.

check.stem: Name the gas released by cattle as they digest grass.
check.modelAnswer: Methane is released by cattle as they digest grass.

check.stem: Explain why CFCs concern environmental scientists despite low volumes.
check.modelAnswer: CFCs concern scientists because they are potent greenhouse gases among the named set, so even small releases add to trapped heat.

check.stem: A nation cuts fossil fuel use but expands rice paddies. Predict its gas profile.
check.modelAnswer: Carbon dioxide emissions fall, but methane emissions rise as the paddy fields release more methane, so its greenhouse profile shifts between the two gases.

glossary.definition: A gas that absorbs infrared radiation so heat stays trapped in the atmosphere.
The greenhouse gas released by cattle as they digest grass and by rice paddy fields.
Fuels such as coal, oil and gas whose combustion releases carbon dioxide.
Chlorofluorocarbons, synthetic gases that act as greenhouse gases.
